title: International Filter Co. v. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Co.
shortTitle: International Filter v. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light
summary: The buyer’s signed order, which by its terms became a contract when approved by an executive officer at the seller’s Chicago office, was the offer, and the executive’s dated “O.K.” was the prescribed acceptance; because the offer designated that act as sufficient, no separate notice of approval was required, and the seller’s acknowledgment letter would have sufficed as notice in any event.
notes: Court: Commission of Appeals of Texas (1925).

sections.Parties: International Filter Company, an Illinois manufacturer of water-purification equipment with its principal office in Chicago, was the plaintiff and the party seeking review. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Company, a Texas company making ice in Conroe, was the defendant. Judge Nickels wrote for Section A of the Texas Commission of Appeals on December 10, 1925, and Chief Justice Cureton adopted the recommended disposition for the Texas Supreme Court.
sections.Material Facts: On February 10, 1920 International Filter’s traveling representative, W. W. Waterman, presented Conroe’s manager, Henry Thompson, with a written proposal for a No. 2 Junior steel-tank water softener and filter at $1,230, f.o.b. Chicago. The form provided that the proposal became a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an executive officer of International Filter at its Chicago office, and that it was submitted for prompt acceptance. Thompson signed an acceptance that day and asked for shipment by March 10. On February 13 P. N. Engel, the company’s president, wrote a dated approval on the paper; on February 14 the company mailed a letter thanking Conroe for the order, confirming the March 10 shipment and asking for a water sample. Conroe received the letter, then tried to cancel on February 28 and again on March 4; International Filter denied any right to cancel on March 2.
sections.Procedural History: International Filter sued for breach. After a trial without a jury the court entered judgment for Conroe on the formation issues and other material issues, and the Court of Civil Appeals affirmed, 269 S.W. 210, agreeing that Engel’s endorsement was an approval within the form but treating the absence of notice as the obstacle. On further review the Commission of Appeals recommended reversal and remand to the intermediate court for questions properly presented but not yet decided, and the Texas Supreme Court adopted that disposition. A favorable ruling on formation therefore did not end the breach action or produce a damages award.
sections.Issue: Who made the legally operative offer, what act accepted it, and did International Filter have to notify Conroe of the executive approval before Conroe lost its power to withdraw? Alternatively, did the February 14 acknowledgment letter communicate approval if notice was required?
sections.Holding: Conroe’s signed order was the offer, even though International Filter drafted the form and called it a proposal, because the form reserved a further act of approval for the seller’s executive officer. Engel’s dated endorsement was approval by an executive officer at the designated place and completed the contract. The writing made that act sufficient and required no separate notice, so the claimed oral demand for prompt notification did not change the written terms. In any event the February 14 letter, read by a reasonable recipient, communicated the approval. The judgment was reversed and the case remanded to the Court of Civil Appeals.
sections.Reasoning: Drafting the form and making the offer are separate roles: because the paper reserved approval by International Filter’s executive, Conroe’s signature supplied the offer. Engel’s dated endorsement was that act. Notice ordinarily protects an offeror who seeks a return promise, but the offeror may dispense with it by authorizing a particular act as sufficient acceptance; drawing on Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., the court held that an offeree completes acceptance by following the method the offer makes sufficient. The writing said the proposal became a contract upon the executive’s approval in Chicago, and requiring notice to arrive in Conroe would add a condition and change both the time and place of formation; the prompt-acceptance clause governed when approval had to occur, not an additional form of acceptance. Alternatively, a notice may communicate acceptance by reasonable implication: the letter thanked the buyer for the specified order, confirmed the shipment and requested the water sample, so a reasonable recipient would understand it to convey approval. Unlike White v. Corlies & Tifft, the offeree here performed an observable act the offer itself made sufficient.

The notes examine control of sales representatives, acknowledgment versus acceptance, and ordinary notice rules for promise-based acceptance.

sections.Parties: International Filter, a machinery seller, sued Conroe Gin, the purchaser, for breach of an agreement for water-treatment equipment.
sections.Material Facts: The seller prepared a $1,230 proposal stating that it became a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an executive officer at the seller’s Chicago office. Conroe signed on February 10. The seller’s officer endorsed “O.K.” on February 13. A February 14 letter thanked Conroe for its order and requested a water sample. Conroe later tried to countermand.
sections.Procedural History: A nonjury trial resulted in judgment for Conroe, affirmed by the Court of Civil Appeals. The Commission of Appeals recommended reversal and remand, adopted by the deciding court, for consideration of other issues not previously resolved.
sections.Issue: Which communication was the offer, which act was acceptance, and was notice of approval required to create the contract?
sections.Holding: Conroe’s executed proposal operated as its offer. The executive’s approval accepted it in the stipulated manner. Separate notice was not required by that offer; alternatively, the February 14 letter sufficiently communicated approval.
sections.Reasoning: The party that drafts a form need not be the offeror. Once Conroe submitted the form for specified approval, its terms defined the act that would complete the bargain. Reading an additional notice condition into that language would change the agreed method. The court distinguishes the act of acceptance from communication reporting the already completed act. The alternative notice holding prevents treating this as blanket permission for entirely private acceptance of every offer.

learning.why: This case prevents a common shortcut: the person who sends the first form is not necessarily the offeror, and an acceptance is not necessarily the communication reporting it.

topics.acceptance: The offer specified executive approval as the operative act.
topics.notice-acceptance: The offer dispensed with separate notice; the letter also supplied notice if needed.
topics.assent: Labels such as “proposal” and “accepted” must be interpreted within the whole sequence.
topics.offer: The buyer made the operative offer on the seller’s form.
